title: Scene Review: Suriya's Loose, Playful Cop Act Carries an Uneven Crime Comedy
excerpt: A star performance worth the ticket, wrapped around a cold case that never quite earns its finale.
body:
• Suriya gives his loosest performance in years — a quirky cop turn that blends comedy with real vulnerability
  • The chemistry between Suriya, Nazriya Nazim and Naslen powers the film's best stretches
  • A second half that keeps losing momentum, and a climax that under-delivers, hold it back
  • Sushin Shyam's score keeps the oddball energy alive even when the case goes cold

Scene is built around a wager: that Suriya, loosening up as a police officer with more quirks than procedures, can carry a Tamil crime comedy that treats its cold case mostly as an excuse for character comedy. For long stretches, the wager pays off. This is the most relaxed the actor has looked on screen in years — playful, unhurried, willing to let a scene breathe — and director Jithu Madhavan builds the film's best material around that ease.

The case itself, a reopened investigation that sets Suriya's officer against Naslen's slippery antagonist, with Nazriya Nazim returning to Tamil cinema alongside them, keeps shifting tone: part procedural, part oddball comedy, part darker thriller. When the blend holds, Scene feels genuinely fresh. When it doesn't, the seams show. The film takes its time settling into its rhythm, the second half keeps stalling, and a climax that should cash in the buildup lands softly. What remains is a star vehicle with a real performance inside it, wrapped around an investigation that never quite earns its finale.

Madhavan's gamble is tonal. Scene keeps asking its audience to hold two registers at once — a police investigation with genuinely dark corners, and a comedy that treats almost everything, including its hero, as slightly absurd. That is a harder film to pull off than a straight thriller, and a more interesting one to watch being attempted. Even where it wobbles, it never feels like product assembled from a template; it feels like a director and a star agreeing to be strange together.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=_nuRAflabx8

What works

Suriya is the film's engine, and the performance is a small reinvention. Instead of the familiar mass-hero template, he plays the officer as an eccentric — funny in a way that keeps brushing against vulnerability, so the comedy has something underneath it. It is the rare star turn that gets more interesting the less it shows off, and the film knows it: scene after scene is arranged to let him riff, react and charm his way through the investigation.

The ensemble around him is well matched. Naslen, stepping away from his boy-next-door image, gives the antagonist a wicked charm that plays beautifully against Suriya's looseness — their scenes together are the film's sharpest. Nazriya Nazim brings an infectious energy to the lighter stretches, and the three-way chemistry carries passages where the plot itself is marking time. Sushin Shyam's score leans into the quirk, keeping the tone buoyant, and the film's vibrant visual style matches its tonal play: this is a good-looking, good-sounding production that understands its own oddball register.

Madhavan's direction deserves its share of the credit. The film is paced like a hangout in its best passages — conversations are allowed to wander, jokes are allowed to land twice — and that looseness is a directorial choice, not an accident. It suits a story about an officer whose method is mostly personality. The risk, of course, is that looseness and drift are the same thing viewed from different seats, and Scene spends its whole running time walking that line.

What doesn't

The investigation is the weakest strand. The narrative coherence frays as the film goes on — threads are picked up and dropped, and the humour that delights early on sometimes crowds out the darker material the story wants to matter. The pacing is the larger problem: slow to settle at the start, and prone to losing momentum through the second half, when a tighter film would be tightening the screws.

And then the climax under-delivers. After a long, deliberately eccentric buildup, the payoff arrives without the weight it needs — the one stretch where Scene plays it safe is the stretch that most needed invention.

There is also a mismatch the film never resolves: the darker the case material gets, the more the comedy has to work to justify itself, and in the later stretches it visibly strains. A version of Scene that trusted its thriller thread more — or committed fully to being a lark — would be a cleaner film. This one wants both, and the wanting shows.

Should you watch it?

Yes, if what you want is Suriya experimenting — this is a performance worth the ticket, inside a comedy that is content to amble. Go in expecting a tight police procedural, though, and the case will frustrate you: the mystery is the pretext, not the point. Scene is in theatres now in Tamil with English subtitles, and runs about two and a half hours.

nri_angle: The film is available with subtitles, making it accessible for non-Tamil speakers, and offers a unique blend of humor and action that may resonate well with fans of Suriya.
author: Diaspora Desk

data_cards.rating_consensus: Suriya's loosest, most playful performance in years carries a crime comedy whose jokes land harder than its investigation — charming and inventive in stretches, uneven in pace, and let down by a climax that doesn't cash its buildup.
